article_title: Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion
citation: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8
title: SGExams multi-year Reddit dataset of student discussions
description: A large-scale corpus of posts and comments from r/SGExams, Singapore's most active youth forum, collected via a custom PRAW pipeline from Jan 2019 to Oct 2023. After filtering post flairs, "a total of 33,291 posts and 571,091 comments from 55,011 users, spanning 12 post flairs remained", consolidated into five broader topics. Validation included a 99.8% retrieval rate against manual counts, demographic verification showing 93.7% of age-indicative users were adolescents aged 13-25, and lexical-semantic uncertainty quantification (weighted F1 = 0.82, κ = 0.91). The raw dataset is shared in the authors' institutional repository with the author field withheld.
requirements: IRB approval with waiver of consent for deidentified, publicly available data; responsible sharing with author field withheld
constraints: Topic labeling relied on the community's initial post flairs, with potential for discussions to drift across topics; diverse flairs lacking commonality were excluded
target_learners: adolescent students in Singapore (secondary school to college)
target_learning_goals: studying curious behaviors and question-posing in naturalistic settings
examples: The dataset supported both macro-level monthly time-series modeling and micro-level parent-child conversational analyses across hours.
key_sources: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8

article_title: Vocabulary Teaching in Foreign Language via Audiovisual Method Technique of Listening and Following Writing Scripts
citation: Ebubekir Bozavlı. (2017). Vocabulary Teaching in Foreign Language via Audiovisual Method Technique of Listening and Following Writing Scripts. International Education Studies, 10(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n5p129
title: SGAV (structuro-global audiovisual) method principles underlying the audiovisual vocabulary treatment
description: The study draws on the SGAV method, which the article says "concentrates on learning verbal language" and rests on two essential principles. The structuro-global aspect holds that learners need both linguistic elements (vocabulary, grammar) and non-linguistic elements (rhythm, stress, gestures, facial expressions) for learning to occur. The audio-visual aspect seeks "simultaneous presentation of voice and image in order to facilitate the comprehension of message". In this study the first aspect was fulfilled through video pronunciations and the second through written transcripts of those pronunciations, though the author modified SGAV's usual priority of spoken language by using spoken and written language simultaneously.
requirements: Provision of the learner with both linguistic and non-linguistic elements
Simultaneous presentation of voice and image
constraints: The research modified SGAV's characteristic priority of spoken language by opting for simultaneous utilisation of spoken and written language
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate foreign language students at C1 level
target_learning_goals: foreign language vocabulary learning and retention
examples: Videos from TV5 Monde's "Enseigner le français avec TV5 Monde" at C1 level were used, with pronunciations transformed into written scripts that participants followed during video projection
key_sources: Ebubekir Bozavlı. (2017). Vocabulary Teaching in Foreign Language via Audiovisual Method Technique of Listening and Following Writing Scripts. International Education Studies, 10(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n5p129

article_title: Student-generated learning materials as active learning: a qualitative study of midwifery students' experiences.
citation: Serhatlıoğlu Seda. (2026). Student-generated learning materials as active learning: a qualitative study of midwifery students’ experiences. BMC Medical Education 26:1504. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09749-9
title: Support student-generated learning material tasks with clear guidance, realistic time allocation, and formative feedback
description: Because SGLM asks students to understand content, design representations, produce materials, and prepare explanations simultaneously, the article argues such tasks can overload working memory and should not be run as minimally guided activities. It concludes that "SGLM activities should be planned with clear guidance, realistic time allocation, formative feedback, and adequate instructional support." In the study itself, the instructor guided topic selection for alignment and diversity while leaving material type and design to student choice.
requirements: Clear instructions and guidance on topic selection
Realistic time planning that accounts for overlapping coursework
Formative feedback and adequate instructional support during preparation
constraints: The article warns that SGLM may increase faculty workload through material review, feedback, exhibition organization, jury evaluation, and rubric-based assessment, so larger-scale applications may need structured timelines, group work, simplified rubrics, and institutional support
target_learners: undergraduate health-professions students, including midwifery students
target_learning_goals: self-confidence and professional awareness through constructing instructional artifacts
examples: The studied course gave students 10 weeks, student-led topic selection with instructor guidance to prevent excessive overlap, encouragement to use low-cost recyclable materials, and an exhibition with jury evaluation excluded from grading
key_sources: Serhatlıoğlu Seda. (2026). Student-generated learning materials as active learning: a qualitative study of midwifery students’ experiences. BMC Medical Education 26:1504. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09749-9

article_title: Medical student experiences of Case-Based Learning (CBL) at a multicultural medical school.
citation: Bruen Catherine, Illing Jan, Daly Ronan, Meagher Frances, Delany Caroline, Offiah Gozie, Doherty Sally, Stuart Ellen, Crehan Martina, Kelly Helen. (2025). Medical student experiences of Case-Based Learning (CBL) at a multicultural medical school. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06585-7
title: Structured Group Feedback Sessions (SGFS) three-stage protocol for curriculum evaluation
description: Structured Group Feedback Sessions, first described by Gibbs et al., are "structured discussions which encourage students to consider and present their views first, then discuss their views with peers while allowing time for individual thought and reflection". The protocol was used here to elicit student perceptions of CBL: stage 1 individual written responses on Post-it notes, stage 2 pair discussion to agree points, stage 3 whole-group discussion with facilitator-guided ranking by importance. Eight sessions of 90 minutes each were held with 36 students.
requirements: A facilitator protocol with three questions written on flip charts
Pilot sessions to refine questions, process and timing
constraints: The authors chose SGFS over interviews to avoid the "dominant voice" and "groupthink"; student rankings were used to remove statements and did not identify an agreed hierarchy
examples: 36 students from 12 nationalities participated in 8 sessions between June and September 2023, a 10.4% response rate from a cohort of 344
key_sources: Bruen Catherine, Illing Jan, Daly Ronan, Meagher Frances, Delany Caroline, Offiah Gozie, Doherty Sally, Stuart Ellen, Crehan Martina, Kelly Helen. (2025). Medical student experiences of Case-Based Learning (CBL) at a multicultural medical school. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06585-7

article_title: Active Learning Outside the Classroom: Implementation and Outcomes of Peer-Led Team-Learning Workshops in Introductory Biology.
citation: Kudish Philip, Shores Robin, McClung Alex, Smulyan Lisa, Vallen Elizabeth A., Siwicki Kathleen K. (2016). Active Learning Outside the Classroom: Implementation and Outcomes of Peer-Led Team-Learning Workshops in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-01-0051
title: Study Group Meeting (SGM) program: a voluntary peer-led team-learning workshop supplementing introductory biology lectures
description: The SGM program is a PLTL-model supplement to two team-taught introductory biology courses at Swarthmore College, fully implemented in 2005–2006. Peer science associates selected from students successful in the course host 2-hour evening workshops twice weekly plus pre-quiz sessions, roughly 30 per semester, where students work in groups of three to seven on faculty-generated challenge questions. The article states that "Defining features of PLTL include peer leaders trained in tutorial methods; challenging questions suitable for collaborative problem solving; and designated meeting times outside lecture." Attendance is strictly voluntary and answers are not collected or graded.
requirements: Peer facilitators trained in pedagogical principles and practices through a weekly seminar course
Faculty-generated challenge questions addressing higher levels of Bloom's taxonomy
Designated meeting space and times outside lecture
constraints: Faculty generally do not attend SGMs
Challenge question answers are not collected or graded
target_learners: First-year introductory biology students, including URM students and students with weaker biology backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of introductory biology lecture material
Ability to articulate solutions to scientific problems
Persistence as biology and STEM majors or minors
examples: SAs facilitate using Socratic questioning, restating student explanations with more appropriate terminology, concept maps, and jigsaw grouping, without providing full answers
key_sources: Kudish Philip, Shores Robin, McClung Alex, Smulyan Lisa, Vallen Elizabeth A., Siwicki Kathleen K. (2016). Active Learning Outside the Classroom: Implementation and Outcomes of Peer-Led Team-Learning Workshops in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-01-0051

article_title: Small-group learning in an upper-level university biology class enhances academic performance and student attitudes toward group work.
citation: Gaudet Andrew D., Ramer Leanne M., Nakonechny Joanne, Cragg Jacquelyn J., Ramer Matt S. (2010). Small-Group Learning in an Upper-Level University Biology Class Enhances Academic Performance and Student Attitudes Toward Group Work. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0015821
title: A small-group learning (SGL) model for upper-level university science courses built on permanent diverse groups, frequent collaborative data-analysis activities, and accountability in evaluation
description: The article describes an SGL model in which permanent, diverse groups of five to six students, formed transparently by subject major, sit and work together throughout the term. Lectures are interspersed with formative group activities at roughly 15-minute intervals in which groups "interpret figures, ... create models based on pertinent data, and ... design experiments." Accountability is built in by requiring individual quizzes before group quizzes and peer evaluation worth 10% of the final grade.
requirements: Permanent instructor-formed, diverse groups (here of five to six students based on subject major) maintained throughout the term
Group activities and quizzes designed so that cooperation facilitates learning, using varied question formats and complex questions with simple answers to enable consensus
Accountability mechanisms: individual completion of quizzes before group submission and peer evaluation included in final marks
constraints: The article did not examine the impact of group composition, activity design, or accountability individually, so their separate effects are untested
Early implementation (Initial SGL, 2007) produced quiz-related anxiety, addressed by moving quizzes to the start of class and covering previous-day material
target_learners: fourth-year undergraduate science students in an elective neurobiology course
target_learning_goals: analysis and evaluation of scientific data
examples: In the Refined SGL sections, each quiz was completed individually and submitted, then the same quiz was completed in groups; group-based evaluations included the group seminar, group quizzes and assignments, and participation
key_sources: Gaudet Andrew D., Ramer Leanne M., Nakonechny Joanne, Cragg Jacquelyn J., Ramer Matt S. (2010). Small-Group Learning in an Upper-Level University Biology Class Enhances Academic Performance and Student Attitudes Toward Group Work. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0015821
